questions.a: When something is working reasonably well, I naturally look for ways to optimise it.
questions.b: When something is working reasonably well, I naturally wonder whether there could be an entirely different way of doing it.

questions.a: Once I have the critical information, I prefer to decide and adjust as more information becomes available.
questions.b: Before committing, I prefer to gather enough information to minimise the chance of overlooking something important.

questions.a: When priorities are unclear, I prefer creating reasonable clarity before investing significant effort.
questions.b: When priorities are unclear, I am comfortable beginning somewhere and allowing clarity to emerge through action.

questions.a: I am willing to sacrifice some predictability when an opportunity appears sufficiently worthwhile.
questions.b: I prefer protecting a strong existing position until a new opportunity becomes reasonably predictable.

questions.a: I am comfortable actively explaining the value my work can create.
questions.b: I prefer allowing the quality of my work to demonstrate its value.

questions.a: I enjoy contributing my expertise inside a larger system where much of the surrounding structure already exists.
questions.b: I enjoy creating the structure around my expertise almost as much as delivering the expertise itself.

questions.a: When experienced people disagree, I first try to understand each point of view.
questions.b: When experienced people disagree, I form my own best view and see how it works in practice.

questions.a: Sudden change makes me curious about what new possibilities might now exist.
questions.b: Sudden change makes me want to establish a dependable new plan quickly.

questions.a: Before investing meaningful time or money in something new, I prefer reasonable evidence that people will value it.
questions.b: I am comfortable making a limited investment in order to discover whether people will value it.

questions.a: In an initial professional conversation, I naturally begin by explaining what I know or can offer.
questions.b: In an initial professional conversation, I naturally spend more time discovering what the other person is trying to solve.

questions.a: I want to turn my expertise into a clear service or offering that clients can directly come to me for.
questions.b: I want to become better known for my expertise within my current professional network or industry.

questions.a: I enjoy situations where part of my work is discovering what the opportunity itself could be.
questions.b: I am usually most effective when I have a reasonably defined outcome to work toward.

questions.a: I generally do my best work when responsibilities and expectations are reasonably explicit.
questions.b: I often do some of my best work when I have room to define what the role or outcome should become.

questions.a: When the potential upside is meaningful enough, I can accept some downside that cannot be completely controlled.
questions.b: When an opportunity offers considerable upside but also meaningful downside, I naturally focus first on protecting the downside.

questions.a: When someone seems hesitant about my recommendation, I usually become curious about what is behind their hesitation.
questions.b: When someone seems hesitant about my recommendation, I usually give them space to think.

questions.a: When I think about my professional future, I naturally think about the kind of role I would like to have.
questions.b: When I think about my professional future, I naturally think about the kind of problem I would like people to seek me out to solve.

questions.a: When I repeatedly encounter a problem, I first try to make the existing process work better.
questions.b: When I repeatedly encounter a problem, I first question whether the existing process needs to exist in its current form.

questions.a: I can feel confident in a decision based partly on experience and judgment even when all the evidence is not yet available.
questions.b: I feel more confident in a decision when I can clearly explain the evidence and logic behind it.

questions.a: When an experiment does not work, I usually become more selective about the next experiment.
questions.b: When an experiment does not work, I usually become curious about what I could change in the next attempt.

questions.a: I am most comfortable discussing commercial terms once the other person has clearly expressed interest.
questions.b: I am comfortable discussing value, scope and commercial expectations relatively early when relevant.

questions.a: I prefer gradually creating the new professional identity through small real-world experiments while continuing my present work.
questions.b: I prefer making a major professional transition once I feel sufficiently prepared for the new role.

questions.a: I generally prefer to share an early version and develop it through other people's reactions.
questions.b: I generally prefer to strengthen an idea considerably before exposing it to others.

questions.a: When a decision carries significant consequences, I naturally examine what could go wrong first.
questions.b: When a decision carries significant consequences, I naturally examine what becomes possible if it succeeds first.

questions.a: In unfamiliar situations, I am comfortable experimenting even when there is little precedent.
questions.b: In unfamiliar situations, I naturally look for something comparable that has worked before.

questions.a: When explaining my work, I naturally emphasise the difference it could make to the other person's situation.
questions.b: When explaining my work, I naturally emphasise the quality of my methodology, knowledge or expertise.

questions.a: Much of my professional motivation comes from becoming excellent at my core area of expertise.
questions.b: I am also interested in activities around the expertise - creating opportunities, relationships, positioning, proposals and business.

questions.a: When I see an interesting opportunity outside my immediate responsibility, I usually keep it in mind until I have sufficient bandwidth.
questions.b: When I see an interesting opportunity outside my immediate responsibility, I tend to explore it even if it was not part of my original plan.

questions.a: When two options seem equally strong, I am inclined to choose one and learn from what follows.
questions.b: When two options seem equally strong, I am inclined to gather another layer of information.

questions.a: When several important variables remain unknown, I tend to delay major commitments until the picture becomes clearer.
questions.b: When several important variables remain unknown, I look for the smallest useful step that can be taken immediately.

questions.a: I prefer making significant professional moves after creating a strong safety buffer.
questions.b: I am comfortable beginning a significant professional move while some parts of the safety net are still being built.

questions.a: When work opportunities are limited, I naturally think about how I could create a need or market for what I can offer.
questions.b: When work opportunities are limited, I naturally look for organisations, roles or networks where my capability could fit.

questions.a: I get satisfaction from discovering value in something other people may not yet have recognised.
questions.b: I get satisfaction from becoming exceptionally good at something that already has recognised value.

questions.a: After making an important decision, I frequently continue checking whether I made the best choice.
questions.b: After making an important decision, I usually redirect my attention toward making the chosen direction work.

questions.a: I can usually redirect my energy relatively quickly when circumstances change.
questions.b: Frequent changes in direction usually require me to consciously reset before I regain momentum.

questions.a: When both the potential loss and potential gain are considerable, the possibility of meaningful advancement weighs heavily in my decision.
questions.b: When both the potential loss and potential gain are considerable, avoiding an unnecessary loss weighs heavily in my decision.

questions.a: When someone says, 'This seems expensive,' my first instinct is to reconsider whether my proposal needs adjusting.
questions.b: When someone says, 'This seems expensive,' my first instinct is to understand what they are comparing the value against.

questions.a: When resources are limited, I tend to first identify what additional support would make the work possible.
questions.b: When resources are limited, I tend to first explore what could be achieved with what is already available.

questions.a: When my judgment differs from that of an experienced person, I am comfortable proceeding when my reasoning still makes sense to me.
questions.b: When my judgment differs from that of an experienced person, I tend to re-examine my reasoning carefully before proceeding.

questions.a: When something unexpected disrupts my plan, my first instinct is to restore stability.
questions.b: When something unexpected disrupts my plan, my first instinct is to reconsider what might now be possible.

questions.a: Before trying something professionally unfamiliar, I prefer seeing credible examples of others who have made it work.
questions.b: I can pursue something professionally unfamiliar even when there are few comparable examples around me.

questions.a: I find it natural to build credibility by making my expertise visible through conversations, networks and professional positioning.
questions.b: I find it more natural to build credibility through consistently delivering excellent work.

questions.a: I can accept variability in the flow of work in exchange for greater freedom over what I build and whom I work with.
questions.b: I would prefer a relatively predictable flow of meaningful work even if someone else controls much of how that work reaches me.

questions.a: I tend to perform at my best when I have clear priorities, defined expectations and a visible standard of success.
questions.b: I tend to perform at my best when I have freedom to shape the priorities, approach and definition of success.

questions.a: I gain more energy from going deeply into a few meaningful challenges.
questions.b: I gain more energy from working across multiple challenges that bring variety and stimulation.

questions.a: I am most engaged when I can use capabilities I already know I am strong at and keep raising the quality of my performance.
questions.b: I am most engaged when I am stretched into unfamiliar territory and have to develop new capabilities while working.

questions.a: I find work most satisfying when I can see a tangible result, achievement or measurable outcome from my effort.
questions.b: I find work most satisfying when I can see that my effort has created meaningful value or positive impact for others.

questions.a: I usually produce my strongest work when I have uninterrupted space to think, create or solve problems independently.
questions.b: I usually produce my strongest work when I can think, create or solve problems through active interaction with others.

questions.a: I stay highly engaged when I receive frequent feedback that helps me adjust while I am working.
questions.b: I stay highly engaged when I have sufficient autonomy to work things through and review the outcome at meaningful milestones.

questions.a: I am naturally drawn toward environments where stability allows me to build mastery, depth and consistency over time.
questions.b: I am naturally drawn toward environments where change, novelty and new possibilities keep me stimulated.

reflections.q: During the last 12 months, what is one opportunity you acted upon that was not explicitly part of your role or responsibilities?
Describe one significant professional decision you made during the last year without having all the information you would ideally have wanted.
Think of a situation where circumstances changed significantly after you had already started. What did you actually do next?
What is one professional risk you deliberately took during the past 12–18 months? What made you decide it was worth taking?
When was the last time you persuaded someone to commit money, time, resources, support or trust to something you proposed?
What is one problem people already approach you to help solve—even when helping them is not formally part of your role?

Think of one professional experience where you felt unusually energised, deeply engaged and highly effective. What were you doing, who were you working with, and what conditions around you made that performance possible?
